results.title: Optus and other telcos 'not meeting needs' of people with complaints over network issues: ombudsman - ABC News
results.content:
After the 64-year-old complained, it started a repetitive cycle where she told her story over and over again while the company failed to fix the problem.

Her phone was tested at the local Optus shop, which showed it was working properly.

She made lengthy calls to call centres from a relative's house and later purchased a Telstra sim card so she could call from home.

"All they could do was sympathise," she said.

As the weeks dragged on, a call centre operator agreed to request checks of the Optus network.

People walk past an Optus store

Judith McLaughlin's phone was found to be operating properly at a local store.(AAP: Bianca De Marchi)

But getting answers would take another month, which caused Ms McLaughlin's frustration to boil over. [...] Two Optus customers have accused the embattled telco of trapping them in a complaint "merry-go-round", as more people demand compensation over lengthy service outages and other serious issues.

The Telecommunications Industry Ombudsman (TIO) told the ABC its data showed Optus and other telcos were "not meeting the needs of people with complaints that take more time and nuance to resolve", with researchers saying the sector rated poorly compared to banking and energy industries.

Judith McLaughlin wasted almost two months pleading with Optus to fix her mobile phone coverage that left her unable to make or receive calls at her Gold Coast home.

> "[It was] a nightmare and it was unrelenting,"

 she said. [...] ## Compensation cases spike

Complaints about Optus have increased 5.7 per cent, according to the latest quarterly stats from the TIO.

While complaints across the sector have only increased slightly, there has been a 16.7 per cent spike in people demanding compensation for stress and inconvenience after they experienced lengthy service outages or other serious problems.

The Consumer Policy Research Centre's Chandni Gupta said the telco sector rated poorly compared to the banking or energy sectors.

"When things fail with the telco's service, there are very few consequences for the telco, but very real ones for customers," Ms Gupta said.

A woman looks at camera with her desk and two screens behind her.

results.title: Optus dominates surge in customer exploitation complaints | Mediaweek
results.content:
The TIO recorded 553 complaints under “unconscionable conduct”, up from 217 the previous year. The category covers conduct that goes beyond ordinary unfairness, including taking advantage of a customer’s vulnerability when selling a product or service.

Optus accounted for 69.8% of those complaints, followed by Telstra at 15.2% and Vodafone at 10.3%.

The figures reflect complaints received, rather than findings that the companies broke the law.

Across the industry, complaints fell 6.5% to 53,834.

The TIO provides free, independent help to customers who can't resolve a dispute with their phone or internet provider.

READ MORE: ACMA takes Optus to court over September 2025 Triple Zero outage

mediaweek

Morning Report

### The leading media trade publication in Australia. [...] ### Getting a response remains the biggest problem

A provider failing to act, or taking too long to act, remained the most common complaint.

It appeared in 33,165 complaints, or 61.6% of the total.

Complaints recorded under “other financial loss” rose 60.7% to 2,609. Network outage complaints increased 28.9% to 1,249.

More customers also complained that providers had failed to properly investigate faults or took too long to connect a service.

Each complaint can involve several issues, meaning the categories overlap.

### Failed emergency calls reported

The TIO received 211 complaints involving people unable to reach Triple Zero or emergency services, or maintain a clear and stable call. [...] Well over 800 other complaints came from customers concerned their service would not work during a future emergency.

Some failed calls occurred before the reporting year, while others involved people testing their access to Triple Zero. Not all complaints were about Optus.

One case involved a 90-year-old woman living alone in remote Western Australia. With no mobile coverage, she depended on a landline that also supported her medical alarm.

When the landline failed, she could neither make a call nor use the alarm during a medical emergency.

The report said she contacted her provider several times, but the fault remained unresolved. She then approached the TIO.
